title: Owners, sudo and umask
summary: Who owns a file, how to act as root safely, and why new files start as 644.

steps.title: Users, groups, chown
body: ```text
$ id
uid=1000(ana) gid=1000(ana) groups=1000(ana),27(sudo),998(docker)
- Users are listed in `/etc/passwd`, groups in `/etc/group`. UID 0 is **root**: the kernel skips permission checks for it.
- `chown user:group file` changes ownership (only root can give files away). `chown -R` recurses. `chgrp group file` changes just the group.
- `sudo usermod -aG docker ana` adds ana to a group. **Log out and in** before it takes effect: groups are read at login.

steps.prompt: Give the web root to the `www-data` user and group, recursively.

steps.title: sudo, and why not to live as root
body: `sudo cmd` runs **one** command as root, after checking `/etc/sudoers` (edit it only with `visudo`, which refuses to save syntax errors that would lock you out).
```bash
sudo systemctl restart nginx     # one privileged action
sudo -i                          # a root shell: use sparingly
sudo -u postgres psql            # run as another user
A classic trap: `sudo echo x > /etc/file` fails, because the **redirection is done by your own shell**, not by sudo. Use `echo x | sudo tee /etc/file` (or `tee -a` to append).

steps.prompt: `sudo echo "10.0.0.5 db" >> /etc/hosts` says *Permission denied*. Which fixes it?
steps.explain: `>>` is performed by your unprivileged shell before sudo runs. `tee` runs under sudo and opens the file itself. Option 2 has the same bug *and* would truncate the file.

steps.title: umask: the default permissions
body: New files start from `666` and new directories from `777`, then the **umask** bits are *removed*.
```text
umask 022       (typical)
dir:   777 & ~022 = 755   rwxr-xr-x
umask 077       (private)
file:  600      dir: 700
It's a mask, not a subtraction: each bit set in the umask is cleared. Set it in `~/.bashrc` or a service's unit file (`UMask=0027`).

steps.prompt: With `umask 027`, what permissions (as rwx) does a newly created **directory** get?
steps.explain: 777 with 027 cleared = 750. `stat -c %A` prints the type character too.

items: `chgrp` to a group the owner belongs to
steps.explain: Owners control the mode bits of their own files. Giving files to someone else, system config and ports below 1024 need root.

steps.title: umask, a shared folder and an ACL
prompt: You share work with your team (group `devs`, which you are in) and with `ana`, who is **not** in that group.
1. Make every new shell of yours create files as `640` and folders as `750` by default: put the right `umask` line
2. Make `~/team` a shared folder: group `devs`, mode `2770` (owner and group get everything, others nothing, and the
**setgid** bit so new files in it belong to `devs` too).
3. Let `ana` read `~/reports/q3.csv` **without** changing its owner, its group or what others get: give her an

checks.name: new shells use umask 027
checks.fail: A new interactive shell does not report `0027` from `umask`. Add `umask 027` to the end of `~/.bashrc`.

checks.name: ~/team belongs to group devs
checks.fail: `~/team` should belong to the group `devs`: `chgrp devs ~/team`.

checks.name: ~/team is 2770
checks.fail: `~/team` should be `rwxrws---` (2770). The leading 2 is setgid.

checks.name: ana can read q3.csv
checks.fail: `ana` still gets *Permission denied*. `setfacl -m u:ana:r ~/reports/q3.csv` adds an entry just for her.

checks.name: others still get nothing
checks.fail: `q3.csv` should still give others nothing (`other::---` in `getfacl`). Use an ACL, not `chmod o+r`.

checks.name: the owner and group did not change
checks.fail: The owner or group of `q3.csv` changed. Leave them, and add an ACL entry instead.

hints: umask takes bits away: from 666 for files and 777 for folders. Removing write for the group and everything for others is `027`. `echo "umask 027" >> ~/.bashrc`.
`chgrp devs ~/team` and `chmod 2770 ~/team` (or `chmod g+s`). Check with `ls -ld ~/team`: the group `x` shows as `s`.
`setfacl -m u:ana:r ~/reports/q3.csv`, then `getfacl ~/reports/q3.csv` shows `user:ana:r--`. `ls -l` adds a `+` after the mode.
explain: `umask` only affects files created **afterwards**, by that process and its children, which is why it goes in a
startup file (or in a service's `UMask=`). The setgid bit on a folder is how shared project folders keep the right
group, so teammates can edit each other's files. ACLs are for the one-off exception, like a single person outside
the group; when you find yourself adding many, a new group is usually cleaner.
